response.text:
Let  

\[
Y=\text{kid's IQ},\qquad X_1=\text{mom's IQ},\qquad X_2=\text{mom's age}.
\]

The fitted multiple regression model is

\[
Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_{1i}+\beta_2X_{2i}+\varepsilon_i.
\]

I will assume the nested ANOVA compares the reduced model \(m_2: Y\sim X_1\) to the full model \(m_1:Y\sim X_1+X_2\), which is the natural comparison for testing whether mom’s age adds predictive power beyond mom’s IQ.

---

### (1) Sample size

The residual degrees of freedom are 431. The full model has 3 parameters: intercept, \(X_1\), and \(X_2\). Thus

\[
n-3=431 \implies n=434.
\]

\[
\boxed{n=434}
\]

---

### (2) Fitted model \(m_1\)

Using the reported least-squares estimates,

\[
\boxed{\widehat{Y}=17.596+0.604X_1+0.388X_2.}
\]

So the fitted regression is

\[
\widehat{\text{kid IQ}}
=
17.596+0.604(\text{mom IQ})+0.388(\text{mom age}).
\]

---

### (3) LS estimate of \(\beta_1\) and interpretation

The least-squares estimate is

\[
\boxed{\hat\beta_1=0.604.}
\]

Interpretation: holding mom’s age fixed, a 1-point increase in mom’s IQ is associated with an estimated increase of about \(0.604\) points in the kid’s IQ.

---

### (4) Test \(H_0:\beta_1=0\) at 5%

We test

\[
H_0:\beta_1=0
\qquad\text{vs.}\qquad
H_1:\beta_1\neq 0.
\]

The test statistic is

\[
t=\frac{\hat\beta_1-0}{SE(\hat\beta_1)}
=
\frac{0.604}{0.0587}
\approx 10.29.
\]

Under \(H_0\),

\[
t\sim t_{431}.
\]

The p-value is extremely small, \(p<2\times 10^{-16}\). Therefore,

\[
\boxed{\text{Reject }H_0.}
\]

There is strong evidence that mom’s IQ is associated with kid’s IQ after adjusting for mom’s age.

---

### (5) Overall \(F\)-statistic for \(m_1\)

The overall test is

\[
H_0:\beta_1=\beta_2=0
\qquad\text{vs.}\qquad
H_1:\text{at least one of }\beta_1,\beta_2\neq 0.
\]

Using

\[
F=\frac{R^2/k}{(1-R^2)/(n-k-1)},
\]

where \(k=2\), \(R^2=0.2036\), and \(n-k-1=431\),

\[
F
=
\frac{0.2036/2}{0.7964/431}
\approx 55.1.
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{F\approx 55.1\text{ on }(2,431)\text{ df}.}
\]

The p-value is very small, \(p<2.2\times 10^{-16}\). The model is significant overall.

---

### (6) \(t\)-statistic for testing \(\beta_2=0\)

\[
t=\frac{\hat\beta_2}{SE(\hat\beta_2)}
=
\frac{0.388}{0.326}
\approx 1.19.
\]

So

\[
\boxed{t\approx 1.19\text{ on }431\text{ df}.}
\]

The corresponding p-value is about \(0.235\), so mom’s age is not significant at the 5% level after adjusting for mom’s IQ.

---

### (7) Hypotheses for the nested ANOVA test

Assuming the nested comparison is

\[
m_2: Y=\alpha_0+\alpha_1X_1+\varepsilon
\]

versus

\[
m_1: Y=\beta_0+\beta_1X_1+\beta_2X_2+\varepsilon,
\]

the ANOVA test is testing whether adding \(X_2\), mom’s age, improves the model.

Thus

\[
H_0:\beta_2=0
\]

versus

\[
H_1:\beta_2\neq 0.
\]

Equivalently, \(H_0\) says mom’s age does not improve the model once mom’s IQ is included.

---

### (8) Blanked ANOVA values and conclusion

The residual standard error is 18.26 on 431 df, so for the full model,

\[
RSS_{\text{full}}=431(18.26)^2\approx 143707.
\]

For a one-variable nested comparison, the partial \(F\)-statistic equals the square of the corresponding \(t\)-statistic:

\[
F=t^2\approx (1.19)^2\approx 1.42.
\]

The numerator df is

\[
432-431=1,
\]

and the denominator df is 431.

The extra sum of squares is

\[
SS_{\text{extra}}=F\cdot MSE
=
1.42(18.26)^2
\approx 472.
\]

So the reduced RSS is approximately

\[
RSS_{\text{reduced}}
=
143707+472
\approx 144180.
\]

The nested ANOVA table is approximately

\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
\text{Model} & \text{Res.Df} & RSS & Df & \text{Sum Sq} & F & p \\
\hline
m_2: Y\sim X_1 & 432 & 144180 & & & & \\
m_1: Y\sim X_1+X_2 & 431 & 143707 & 1 & 472 & 1.42 & 0.235
\end{array}
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{F\approx 1.42,\quad df=(1,431),\quad p\approx 0.235.}
\]

Since \(p\approx 0.235>0.05\), we fail to reject \(H_0\). There is not sufficient evidence that mom’s age improves prediction of kid’s IQ after mom’s IQ is already in the model.
